extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent attorneys, and law students drafting or defending patent-infringement actions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for drafting declarations and for the pleading of defenses in actions for patent infringement (who must be named, what facts must be averred, what defenses may be pleaded and notice/timing requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Person 'interested' for damages (standing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The words 'person or persons interested' mean the person(s) interested in the patent at the time when the infringement was committed (the cause of action for which damages may be recovered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignee or grantee is not interested in damages for infringement committed before sale/transfer. The plaintiff must be interested at the time of the infringing act to recover damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executor/administrator capacity to sue
rubrics_metrics.description: An executor who proves the will and receives letters of administration, or who is given power to act independently, can maintain an action for infringement in his character as executor/administrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent was surrendered and a reissue made to such executor in the same character (specific grant), the executor/grantee may have exclusive legal title and sustain suit as if designated as trustee rather than executor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of covenants re: renewals/extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: A covenant by a patentee made prior to the law authorizing extensions does not necessarily include administrator extensions under later statute; covenants are construed to include renewals obtained upon surrender for defective specification only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A covenantee will not automatically obtain benefits of extensions obtained by an administrator under the act of 1836 unless the covenant expressly or by construction covers such extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration must show title with convenient certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration in an action for infringement should show a title in the plaintiff with convenient certainty and set forth all matters which are of the essence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without these allegations the plaintiff fails to show a legal right to judgment. Several parts of the declaration should be considered in order; profert of letters-patent and specification (when produced) are part of the declaration and provide necessary certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aver original and first inventor status
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration should commence with a recital that the plaintiff was 'the original and first inventor' of the subject-matter complained of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This averment is necessary despite the letters-patent reciting the same, because the plaintiff must be able affirmatively to show at trial that he was the original inventor; letters-patent are only prima facie evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aver novelty and utility and absence of prior public use/sale
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration should aver that the subject-matter was 'new and useful,' 'not known or used before the plaintiff's invention or discovery,' and 'not at the time of his application for a patent in public use or on sale with his consent or allowance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These averments tender issue on novelty and utility; want of novelty is a defense enumerated in the statute and must be put in issue appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: No need to specify exact time of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary to aver at what specific time the invention was made; it suffices to aver that it was made before the application for the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The declaration need only show invention prior to application; exact dates need not be pleaded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aver citizenship and formal issuance of letters-patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Although whether citizenship must be averred is undetermined, in practice it is generally done and is safest; it is absolutely necessary to aver that the plaintiff obtained letters-patent in due form of law under the public seal and with the required signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While citizenship averment may be safer than omission, the declaration must aver that the patent was granted in due form (signed/countersigned) and that the patent actually issued or was delivered as usual practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: No need to plead preliminary Patent Office proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration need not show the regularity of the preliminary proceedings in the Patent Office that led to the grant; it may simply aver that the grant was duly obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grant (letters-patent) is itself sufficient evidence that required preliminary steps were properly taken; courts will presume regularity on demurrer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set forth substance of grant and profert of letters-patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The substance of the grant should be set forth — that the letters-patent secured to the plaintiff the exclusive right for the statutory term — and profert of the letters-patent should be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A description in the words of the patent is sufficient and it is not necessary to set forth the specification in the declaration; a defendant may obtain the specification in the record by praying oyer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allege value, breach, and damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration should conclude with an averment of the value of the patent right, the breach by the defendant, and the damages sustained by the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual damages may be alleged in gross; in actions at law, a breach must be established that occurred before suit (equity differs as to injunctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Breach must have occurred before suit in action at law
rubrics_metrics.description: In an action at law for breach of a patent right, it is indispensable to establish a breach before the suit is brought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity differs: a bill for an injunction may lie upon sufficient proof of intent to violate the patent even absent completed breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: No need to plead statutory form of the offense
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration need not set forth the act complained of as contrary to statute; it may simply allege that the defendant 'made, constructed, used, and vended' the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statutory mode of pleading is necessary when suing for a penalty, but for damages a simple allegation of the infringing acts suffices. Reiterated infringements may be joined in one action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated infringements recoverable in single action
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated infringements of a patent may be sued for and recompensed in one action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no doctrine requiring splitting of grievances of the same character into separate actions; evidence will address temporal scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee plaintiff must plead chain of title and recording
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff sues in the character of assignee, he must set forth both the patentee's title and his own, and should aver that the assignments were duly recorded in the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the declaration omits to state that assignments were recorded, the omission may be cured by verdict if the general terms of the declaration otherwise authorize proof of recording at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of recording of assignment may be given before or after action
rubrics_metrics.description: At trial, proof may be given of the recording of an assignment either before or after the action was brought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore the declaration need not necessarily aver recording within statutory period; the recording can be proved in evidence at appropriate time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant may plead general issue and give statute/special matter with 30-day notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the fifteen section of the Act of 1836, the defendant may plead the general issue and give the statute and any special matter in evidence, provided he gives written notice of such special matters to the plaintiff or his attorney thirty days before trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice substitutes for a special plea and is required to protect the plaintiff from surprise; the defendant may alternatively plead specially (in which case the plea itself is notice). The notice must be strictly construed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing requirement for pleading special matters (30 days)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the defendant pleads specially or under the general issue with notice, the special plea or the notice must be filed or given thirty days before the term or trial, or the plaintiff will be entitled to a continuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plaintiff has a right to the thirty days to prepare; this applies whether set up by plea or by notice under the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: When relying on prior invention/use, must state names/places/residences
rubrics_metrics.description: When the defendant relies on prior invention, knowledge, or use of the thing patented, he shall state in his notice the names and places of residence of those whom he intends to prove possessed prior knowledge and where the same thing had been used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision was added to prevent surprise and to place particulars on the record; failure to specify places or names precludes offering evidence of other places (notice strictly construed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict construction of notice (geographic/scope limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice of special matter must be strictly construed; specifying prior use 'in the United States' will not allow evidence of prior use in England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice limits the scope of evidence; the courts will enforce that limitation to prevent unfair surprise to the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses available under general issue without notice — noninfringement/license
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the general issue and without special notice, the defendant may show he never did the act complained of (noninfringement) or that he was acting under a license or purchase from the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are ordinary issues of fact that the defendant may plead and prove without following the statute's notice provision for special matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses available under general issue without notice — plaintiff alien/title/formal defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the general issue without notice, the defendant may show that the plaintiff is an alien not entitled to a patent, that the plaintiff lacks a good title as assignee, or that the patent was not duly issued according to law (signatures, seal, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are defenses touching standing, title and formal issuance that may be raised under 'not guilty' without the special notice procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense that subject is not patentable (not art/machine/manufacture/comp of matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Admitting novelty, the defendant may show under the general issue without notice that the invention is not a patentable subject (i.e., not an 'art, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter' within the statute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is distinct from want of novelty (which is a statutory defense requiring notice). The issue is necessarily raised by a plea of 'not guilty.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of novelty requires statutory notice
rubrics_metrics.description: A defense of lack of novelty (prior description or prior public use/sale) falls under the statute and must be specified in the defendant's notice when pleading under the general issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior description/use/sale are among the enumerated special matters for which notice is required; the statute contemplates specificity (names/places) for such defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of utility as defense (worthless/frivolous invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the general issue without notice the defendant may show that, though new, the invention fails in point of utility and is worthless or frivolous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Want of utility is a clear bar to the action and may be relied on without invoking the statute's notice procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification absence or ambiguity voids patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may show that there is no specification, or that the specification is so ambiguous and unintelligible that the court cannot determine what the intended invention is; if so, the patent is void for ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear and distinct specification is essential to patent validity; this issue is different from the statutory concealment/addition issue and may be raised under the plea of not guilty without notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory special defense — concealment or addition with intent to deceive
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute permits the defendant (with proper notice) to show that the description and specification do not contain the whole truth or contain more than is necessary to produce the described effect, and that such concealment or addition was made for the purpose of deceiving the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This issue is distinguishable from mere ambiguity; historically courts have considered whether lack of enablement/defect in specification voids the patent only if accompanied by intent to deceive. The statute contemplates that proof of such deceit (and particulars) be put on the record by notice.
